title: The Bandgap Principle
intro: A reference that does not drift with temperature is built by adding two voltages whose temperature coefficients cancel. Bipolar junctions provide both, reproducibly, even in a pure CMOS process (Razavi, Section 12.3).

blocks.text: Zero TC from opposite TCs

If $V_1$ falls with temperature and $V_2$ rises, choose weights so that $\alpha_1 \partial V_1/\partial T + \alpha_2 \partial V_2/\partial T = 0$; then $V_{REF} = \alpha_1 V_1 + \alpha_2 V_2$ has zero first-order temperature coefficient. Since most process parameters themselves drift with temperature, a circuit that is temperature-stable tends to be process-stable as well.
The negative-TC voltage: $V_{BE}$

For a bipolar device $I_C = I_S \exp(V_{BE}/V_T)$, and the saturation current depends strongly on temperature through the intrinsic carrier density and mobility ($\mu \propto T^m$ with $m \approx -3/2$, $n_i^2 \propto T^3 \exp(-E_g/kT)$):
Differentiating $V_{BE} = V_T \ln(I_C/I_S)$ with $I_C$ held constant gives

blocks.caption: With $V_{BE} = 750$ mV, $T = 300$ K, $E_g = 1.12$ eV: about $-1.5$ mV/K.

blocks.text: The slope depends on $V_{BE}$ and on $T$ itself, so $V_{BE}$ is not a straight line in temperature; this is the source of bandgap curvature.
The positive-TC voltage: $\Delta V_{BE}$

Run two identical transistors at collector currents $nI_0$ and $I_0$ (or equal currents into devices whose areas differ by $n$). Their base-emitter voltages differ by a quantity that depends only on $V_T$:

blocks.tex: \Delta V_{BE} = V_T \ln n, \qquad \frac{\partial \Delta V_{BE}}{\partial T} = \frac{k}{q}\ln n

blocks.text: This TC is independent of temperature and of how the collector currents themselves vary. If the current ratio is $n$ and the area ratio is $m$, the current densities differ by $nm$ and $\Delta V_{BE} = V_T \ln(nm)$. Cancelling $-1.5$ mV/K with $\Delta V_{BE}$ alone would need $\ln n \approx 17.4$, i.e. $n$ of order $3\times 10^{7}$, so in practice the small $\Delta V_{BE}$ is amplified by a resistor ratio instead.
The op-amp bandgap core

blocks.alt: Schematic. An op amp A1, pointing up, drives a top line that is the output Vout. From that line R1 runs down to node X, which is the emitter of a diode-connected substrate pnp Q1 of unit size. Also from the line, R2 runs down to node Y and then R3 continues to the emitter of Q2, which has n units. Base and collector of both pnps are grounded. X goes to the op amp's plus input and Y to its minus input.
blocks.caption: The classic core: the op amp holds X and Y equal, so $V_T\ln n$ appears across $R_3$ and is amplified by $1 + R_2/R_3$.

blocks.text: With $R_1 = R_2$ the op amp forces $V_X = V_Y$, so both branches carry the same current and $V_{BE1} - V_{BE2} = V_T \ln n$ sits across $R_3$. That PTAT current also flows in $R_2$:

blocks.caption: Zero TC when $(1 + R_2/R_3)\ln n \approx 17.4$, e.g. $n = 8$ and $R_2/R_3 \approx 7.4$.

blocks.text: Note what the circuit does not try to do: node Y (about one $V_{BE}$) is not temperature-stable; only the op-amp output, which adds an amplified PTAT drop to $V_{BE2}$, is. The result depends on resistor ratios only, so the absolute resistor TC cancels. Written from the other branch, $V_{out} = V_{BE1} + (R_1/R_3)V_T\ln n$, which is consistent because $V_{BE1}$ itself carries an extra $+(k/q)\ln n$ of slope.
Why it is called a bandgap
Set $\partial V_{REF}/\partial T = 0$ in $V_{REF} = V_{BE} + V_T \ln n$ (any amplification lumped into $n$), use the $V_{BE}$ slope above, and substitute back:

The zero-TC value is fixed by fundamental quantities: about $1.12 + 2.5 \times 0.0259 \approx 1.18$ V for $m = -1.5$ at 300 K, and practical circuits land between 1.2 and 1.25 V. As $T \to 0$ the reference tends to $E_g/q$, the silicon bandgap, hence the name.
Try it

Drag the multiplier: below about 8.4 (for $n = 8$) the sum falls with temperature, above it rises; at the right value the curve is flat, leaving only the small second-order bow that comes from the curvature of the real $V_{BE}$.

blocks.title: The $V_{BE}$ temperature coefficient
blocks.text: Evaluate $\partial V_{BE}/\partial T$ at 300 K for $V_{BE} = 0.75$ V, $m = -1.5$, $E_g/q = 1.12$ V. Repeat for $V_{BE} = 0.65$ V.
solution: At 0.65 V: $(0.65 - 0.0646 - 1.12)/300 = -1.78$ mV/K. A lower current density (smaller $V_{BE}$) gives a steeper slope.
